notes.meaning: God pronounces sorrow and doom on Nineveh, calling it a city of blood. It was a place built on murder, deceit, and endless robbery. The Assyrians never grew tired of plundering their neighbours, but God will not let their violence go unpunished.

The prophet hears the sudden, terrifying sounds of the invading army breaking into the city. Whips crack to urge the chariot horses forward, wheels rattle loudly over the stones, and war chariots leap across the ground. The attackers move with furious speed to strike down Nineveh.

Mounted soldiers charge into battle with blazing swords and glittering spears. A massive slaughter follows, leaving mountains of dead bodies across the streets. The corpses pile up so high that both the soldiers and the survivors stumble over them.

Nineveh is pictured as an attractive prostitute and sorceress who lures people into a trap. Through flattering promises, wealthy trade, and dishonest alliances, Assyria charmed smaller nations only to strip away their freedom and enslave them. God brings ruin on her because her polite diplomacy was really a selfish scheme to conquer others.

The Lord of Hosts declares that He is directly against Nineveh. Just as an unfaithful woman was publicly exposed and shamed in ancient times, God will pull her royal skirts over her face. Surrounding kingdoms will see all her pride stripped away, leaving her completely humiliated.

God promises to pelt Nineveh with foul dirt and treat her with total contempt. She will be put on public display like a criminal locked in a pillory for all to mock. Her grand reputation will be dragged through the mud for the whole world to see.

Everyone who looks at the ruined city will turn away in disgust and shock. People will ask who could possibly mourn for Nineveh, since she never showed mercy to anyone else. No one will step forward to comfort a tyrant that made the whole earth suffer.

Nineveh is asked if she thinks she is any safer than the famous Egyptian city of Thebes. That great capital sat securely along the Nile River, protected on every side by broad waters that acted like a fortress wall. Yet despite having water as its shield, that mighty city still fell.

Thebes seemed impossible to conquer because her military strength and allies were boundless. She was supported by the armies of Ethiopia and Egypt, along with troops from Put and Libya. Even with all those powerful nations standing beside her, human strength could not protect her from judgment.

In spite of all her strength, Thebes was conquered and led away into slavery. The enemy brutally smashed her infants in the streets and threw dice to divide her noble leaders as prisoners in chains. Nineveh is warned that the very cruelty she inflicted on others will now happen to her.

Nineveh will drink the bitter cup of God's anger and stagger around like a drunkard. Fear will make her proud citizens run to hide from the attacking armies. In their panic, they will search desperately for help from neighbours, but none will come.

Assyria's fortresses are compared to fig trees full of ripe, early figs. Just as ripe fruit drops straight into a person's mouth with only a gentle shake of the branch, her strongholds will fall quickly to the enemy. No earthly wall can keep out the judgment of God.

Assyria's fierce warriors will lose all their bravery and become completely helpless in the fight. The mountain passes and fortified entrances to the land will open wide to the invaders. Fire will burn through the heavy wooden bars that held the city gates shut.

The prophet sarcastically tells Nineveh to get ready for a long, hard siege. He urges them to store plenty of water, stomp the mud to mix mortar, and fire up the kilns to bake fresh bricks for their broken walls. Yet all their frantic preparations will fail to save them.

Right inside the defences they worked so hard to build, fire and the sword will destroy them. The enemy will wipe them out just as hungry young locusts devour an entire green field. Even if Nineveh raises a massive army as thick as a locust swarm, it will do no good.

Nineveh had filled its markets with merchants, making them as countless as the stars in the night sky. Yet like a swarm of locusts that strips a field bare and quickly flies away, these traders will take their wealth and disappear. When trouble comes, fair-weather friends vanish and offer no real help.

Assyria's crown princes and army commanders are compared to locusts resting on stone walls during a cold day. As soon as the sun rises and warms the air, the insects take flight and vanish into nowhere. In the same way, Nineveh's top leaders will scatter and disappear when the heat of battle arrives.

The prophet calls out to the king of Assyria, telling him that his royal leaders and governors are sleeping the sleep of death. With their leaders lying dead, the common people are scattered over the mountains like sheep without a shepherd. There is no one left to call them together or rebuild the kingdom.

Nineveh's wound is fatal, and there is no medicine or hope to heal her broken empire. Every nation that hears news of her ruin will clap their hands with relief and joy. Because everyone had suffered from Assyria's constant cruelty, the whole world rejoices that her wicked reign is finally finished.
